context: Lisa is chatting about living in a big city.

context: Emma is giving her brother advice before his exam.

context: Sam is talking about a party he skipped last night.

context: Rina is daydreaming at her desk on a busy Monday.

context: Tom missed the train this morning.

context: Dana is stuck at home with a broken laptop.

context: Ben is tired of the noise in his flat.

context: Lena is talking about her friend Omar, who moved abroad.

context: Sara hates her phone, which keeps freezing.
prompt: I wish this phone ___ so slow. It's driving me crazy!
why: Wishing a present fact were different takes the past simple (was or were).

context: Jake is annoyed that his friend always shows up late.
prompt: I wish you ___ me when you're going to be late.
why: Wish + would is for a habit that annoys you and that you want someone to change.

context: Nina is speaking about her brother, who is great at cooking.
prompt: If he ___ cooking classes as a teenager, he wouldn't be so good in the kitchen today.
why: Imagining a different past gives past perfect; the result today uses would + base verb.

context: Chris thinks about yesterday's picnic, which got cancelled because of the rain.
prompt: I wish it ___ yesterday. We could have had a great picnic.
why: Regret about a finished past event (yesterday) takes wish + past perfect.

context: Maya talks about her friend Yael, who has always been very shy.
prompt: If Yael ___ so shy, she ___ more friends back in school.
why: Yael is still shy (present), but the result is in the past: past simple in the if-part, would have + past participle in the result.

context: Eli has a test tomorrow and still isn't ready.
prompt: If I ___ harder last week, I ___ so stressed right now.
why: Last week is past, so use past perfect; right now is present, so use would be.

context: Dana missed her flight this morning because she left home late.
prompt: If she ___ earlier, she ___ in Rome by now.
why: Past condition (had left) with a result that is true now (by now) needs 'would be'.

context: Tom is stuck at home with a cold and wants to be at the party.
prompt: I wish I ___ so sick right now, because I'd love to go out.
why: To wish something were different right now, use the past tense: 'I wish I wasn't'.

context: Lena is still angry about a mistake she made at work last week.
prompt: I wish I ___ that email to the whole team last Friday.
why: To regret something in the past, use 'wish' with the past perfect (had + past participle).

context: Sam never studied for his driving test, so he doesn't have a license now.
prompt: If Sam ___ for the test back then, he ___ his own car today.
options: had studied / would have been having
why: Past condition needs had studied; a result true today uses 'would' plus the base verb.

context: Maya is annoyed that her neighbor plays loud music every night.
prompt: I wish my neighbor ___ the music down at night.
why: We use 'wish ... would' to complain about someone's annoying habit and ask for change.

context: Ben is tired today because he stayed up late binge-watching a show last night.
prompt: If I ___ up so late last night, I ___ so tired right now.
why: Last night is past (hadn't stayed). Being tired right now is present, so 'wouldn't be'.

context: Noa lives far from the city and spends two hours a day commuting.
prompt: I wish I ___ closer to the office. Then I'd have more free time.
why: To wish a present situation were different, use the past tense: 'I wish I lived'.

context: Jake isn't a great cook because he never took lessons as a kid.
prompt: If my parents ___ me to cooking classes, I ___ a much better cook now.
why: A past 'if' (had sent) with a result that's true now needs 'would be'.

context: Rita forgot her friend's birthday yesterday and feels terrible.
prompt: I wish I ___ her birthday yesterday. Then she wouldn't be upset today.
why: Yesterday is finished, so use 'wish' with the past perfect to show regret.

context: Chris took a job abroad years ago and now misses his family.
prompt: If I ___ that job offer, I ___ near my family today.
why: Past choice needs had not taken; living near family today is a present result: 'would be living'.

context: Dan missed his flight this morning.
prompt: If I ___ up earlier this morning, I wouldn't be stuck at the airport now.
why: Waking up is a past action with a result now. Use 'had + past participle' in the if-part and 'would + base verb' in the result.

context: Maya takes the bus to work every day and really hates it.
prompt: I wish I ___ a car, so I wouldn't have to take the bus every day.
why: To wish for a different situation right now, use the past tense after 'wish'.

context: Tom failed the driving test yesterday.
prompt: I wish I ___ the test yesterday. Now I have to wait another month.
why: For a wish about a past event, use past perfect. 'Yesterday' shows it is already over.

context: Lisa lives far from her friends.
prompt: If she ___ closer to the city, she would have joined us last night.
why: Where she lives is true in general, so the if-part uses past simple. The result is in the past: 'would have joined'.

context: Sam is annoyed that his neighbor is so loud every night.
prompt: I wish my neighbor ___ the music so loud every night.
why: To complain about someone's annoying habit, use 'wish + would'. Here it means 'I want them to stop'.

context: Nina studied art instead of business. She's not happy with her job now.
prompt: If I ___ business at university, I would have a better job today.
why: The past choice (university) changes the present (job today). Use past perfect in the if-part, 'would + base verb' for the result.

context: Ben forgot his friend's birthday last week.
prompt: I wish I ___ Jake's birthday last Friday. He's still upset with me.
why: A wish about a past mistake needs past perfect. 'Last Friday' shows the event is finished.

context: Chloe doesn't speak Spanish, so she couldn't help the tourists yesterday.
prompt: If I ___ Spanish, I would have helped those tourists yesterday.
why: Speaking Spanish is a general ability now, so use past simple in the if-part. The result is in the past: 'would have helped'.

context: It's raining hard, and Omar left his umbrella at home.
prompt: I wish I ___ my umbrella this morning. I'm soaking wet now.
why: A wish about a past action uses past perfect. 'This morning' is finished, and the result is now.

context: Emma is stressed because she has too much work.
prompt: If she ___ so many projects last month, she wouldn't be so busy now.
why: A past action ('last month') causes a present result. Use past perfect in the if-part, 'would + base verb' for the result.

context: Maya is talking about her new phone.
prompt: My phone ___ in a taxi last night, so I had to buy a new one.
why: Past passive: the phone didn't do the stealing, and 'last night' is a finished time, so we use 'was + past participle'.

context: Dan is checking on the office renovation.
prompt: Don't go in there. The floor ___ right now.
why: Present continuous passive: the painting is happening right now, and the floor receives the action.

context: Noa is asking about a package she's waiting for.
prompt: Good news! Your order ___ and it will arrive tomorrow.
why: Present perfect passive: the sending is done and the result matters now. The order can't send itself.

context: Liam is explaining why the party was moved.
prompt: We couldn't use the garden because it ___ for a wedding that weekend.
why: Past perfect passive: the booking happened before the time we're talking about, and the garden was booked by someone else.

context: Tom is talking about next month's event.
prompt: Don't worry about the tickets. They ___ to everyone by Friday.
why: Future passive: it's a prediction about something that will happen, and the tickets receive the action.

context: Sara is telling a friend about her office building.
prompt: This building ___ in 1998, and it still looks great.
why: Past passive: '1998' is a finished point in time, so we use the simple past, not the present perfect.

context: Yossi is complaining about his street.
prompt: The road outside my house ___ right now. It's so noisy!
why: Present continuous passive: 'right now' means the work is still going on, and workers are doing it, not the road.

context: Emma is describing how her favorite café works.
prompt: At this café, the bread ___ fresh every morning.
why: Present simple passive: it's a regular habit, 'every morning', and the bread doesn't bake itself.

context: Ben is telling a friend about his trip to the airport.
prompt: I couldn't get on the plane because my flight ___ when I got there.
why: Past perfect passive: the cancelling happened before he arrived, and someone else cancelled the flight.

context: Lena is calling a friend about a lost bag.
prompt: Don't worry, your bag ___ by the airline and they'll deliver it tonight.
why: Present perfect passive: the finding is done and it matters now, since the delivery is coming tonight.

context: Dana is talking about her new office.
prompt: The whole building ___ last year, so everything looks brand new.
why: Last year is a finished past time, and someone else did the painting, so we use the past simple passive: was + past participle.

context: Tom is checking his online order.
prompt: Good news! My package ___ already ___, so it should arrive tomorrow.
why: 'Already' links the past action to now, and someone else sent the package, so we use the present perfect passive: has been + past participle.

context: Noa is chatting about a school event.
prompt: The party ___ next Friday if the weather is good.
why: It is a future plan and the party doesn't act, so we use will be + past participle.

context: Liam is explaining why he was late.
prompt: I couldn't get into the room because the door ___ when I got there.
why: The locking happened before I got there, so we use the past perfect passive: had been + past participle.

context: Maya is talking about her street.
prompt: Our street ___ every morning at six, so it's really noisy.
why: Every morning shows a regular habit, so we use the present simple passive: is + past participle.

context: Omer is looking at a photo from his childhood.
prompt: This photo ___ in 2009, when I was ten.
why: In 2009 is a specific past time, so we use the past simple passive: was + past participle.

context: Rachel is on the phone with a friend at the mall.
prompt: Sorry, I can't talk. My name ___ over the speaker right now.
why: Right now the action is happening, so we use the present continuous passive: is being + past participle.

context: Yuval is talking about a new app.
prompt: By the end of this month, the new app ___ by over a million people.
why: By the end of this month points to a future deadline, so we use will have been + past participle.

context: Emma is talking about her old bike.
prompt: I used to love my bike, but it ___ last week, so now I walk.
why: Last week is a finished past time, so we use the past simple passive: was + past participle.

context: Talking about a hotel room in Lisbon.
prompt: The room ___ every morning by the staff, so it was always spotless.
why: Past habit, and the room doesn't clean itself: use past simple passive, was + past participle.

context: Two coworkers talk about a delayed project.
prompt: Sorry, the report isn't ready yet. It ___ right now.
why: It's happening right now, and the report receives the action: is being + past participle.

context: A friend asks about your new phone.
prompt: I love it! It ___ to me last week by my cousin.
why: "Last week" is a finished time, so use past simple passive.

context: Talking about a famous pizza place in Rome.
prompt: This restaurant ___ in 1985 by a young couple, and it's still very popular.
why: 1985 is a finished past time, and "by a young couple" tells us who did it: past simple passive, was + past participle.

context: A teacher talks to her class before a trip.
prompt: Don't worry, all the tickets ___ already ___ by the school.
why: "Already" connects past to now, and the tickets receive the action: present perfect passive, have been + past participle.

context: Sam is explaining why his street is noisy.
prompt: Right now the road ___ , so we can't park outside.
why: The work is in progress now, and the road receives the action: is being repaired.

context: Emma tells her friend about her lost bag.
prompt: Good news! My bag ___ at the train station yesterday.
why: "Yesterday" is finished past, and the bag didn't do the finding: was found.

context: Planning a party with a roommate.
prompt: Don't stress about the music. It ___ by Dan tomorrow night.
why: "Tomorrow" points to the future, and the music receives the action: will be + past participle.

context: Chatting about a movie everyone is talking about.
prompt: By the time we got to the cinema, all the tickets ___ .
why: The selling happened before we arrived, so use past perfect passive: had been sold.

context: A manager updates the team about a new office.

why: "Next month" is future and the office receives the action: will be finished.

context: Maya's phone fell in the pool yesterday. She's talking to her friend about it.
prompt: I took it to the shop this morning, and it ___ right now.
why: Right now, an action in progress, done to the phone by someone else: present continuous passive.

context: Tom is reading the news about the bridges in his city.
prompt: The old bridge ___ in 1950, and it's still used every day.

context: Dana is calling the shop about a package she's waiting for.
prompt: Hi, I ordered a laptop last week, but it ___ yet.
why: "Yet" connects the past to now, and the laptop receives the action: present perfect passive.

context: Dana is telling a friend about a meeting last week.
prompt: My boss said he ___ late for the meeting, but he came early!
why: The meeting is over, so we report his 'will' as 'would'.

context: Tom is explaining why he missed the bus.
prompt: I told my sister that I ___ my keys at home.
why: The leaving happened before the telling, so reported speech uses the past perfect.

context: Lina is chatting about her new flatmate.
prompt: She said she ___ in London for five years before moving here.
why: The living came before the moving, so we use the past perfect in reported speech.

context: Mark is telling a coworker about his doctor's visit.
prompt: The doctor told me that I ___ more water every day.
why: 'Should' stays the same in reported speech and is followed by the basic form of the verb.

context: Noa is talking about a text from her friend Yael.
prompt: Yael asked me if I ___ to the party the night before.
why: A question about an earlier event, reported in the past, uses the past perfect.

context: Sam is telling his mom about his teacher.
prompt: My teacher said that she ___ our tests the next day.
why: When reporting a plan for the future, 'will' becomes 'would'.

context: Ben is describing a message he got from his landlord.
prompt: He said that he ___ the heating that week, but nobody came.
why: 'Is going to' becomes 'was going to' when we report it in the past.

context: Maya is telling a friend about her brother's call.
prompt: My brother said he ___ me when he got to the airport.
why: A promise about the future, reported in the past, uses 'would'.

context: Omar is talking about a new colleague.
prompt: She told me she ___ a car, so she took the train to work.
why: 'Have' as ownership is a state, so 'don't have' becomes the past simple 'didn't have'.

context: Eli is talking about a shop assistant.
prompt: I asked her when the store ___, and she said at nine.
why: A question about a regular schedule, reported in the past, uses the past simple.

context: Dana is telling a friend about a phone call she had this morning.
prompt: My boss called and said he ___ late for the meeting, but he came on time.
why: In reported speech, 'will' moves back to 'would' when the original words were said in the past.

context: Tom is explaining why he missed the party last night.
prompt: I told my friends that I ___ sick all day.
why: The sick time was before the moment of speaking in the past, so we use the past perfect.

context: Noa is telling her sister what the teacher said yesterday.
prompt: The teacher said that we ___ the test the next day.
why: A future plan said in the past becomes 'would' in reported speech.

context: Liam is talking about a text from his cousin.
prompt: He wrote that he ___ at the airport at that moment.
why: 'Is waiting' moves back one step to 'was waiting' when we report a past message.

context: Maya is telling her roommate about a chat with the landlord last month.
prompt: Last month, he asked me if I ___ the rent already.
why: 'Already' shows an earlier action, and reported questions step back to the past perfect.

context: Eli is describing what his coach told him after practice.
prompt: She said I ___ harder if I wanted to make the team.
why: 'Have to' becomes 'had to' in reported speech after a past verb like 'said'.

context: Shira is telling a friend about her brother's phone call from abroad.
prompt: He said he ___ home the following week.
why: 'Following week' shows a future plan, so 'is coming' goes back to 'was coming'.

context: Ben is explaining a message from the airline.
prompt: They told us that our flight ___ two hours earlier.
why: The cancelling happened before the message, and 'has been cancelled' steps back to the past perfect.

context: Yael is chatting about her new neighbor.
prompt: She mentioned that she ___ in Chicago for ten years before moving here.
why: The living came before the move, and both were in the past, so we use the past perfect.

context: Omer is telling his dad about a conversation with his manager last week.
prompt: Last week, my manager asked me whether I ___ time to help with the project that day.
why: A reported 'do you have' question moves back to simple past after 'asked'.

context: Noa texted you: "I'm leaving now."
prompt: Noa told me she ___ leaving right then.
why: When we report what someone said in the past, the present tense usually moves back one step: 'is' becomes 'was'.

context: Tom said, "I lost my keys." That's why he couldn't get in.
prompt: Tom said he ___ his keys, so he couldn't get in.
why: Reporting a past action from earlier means going one step further back: 'lost' becomes 'had lost'.

context: Mia said, "I will call you tomorrow."
prompt: Mia promised she ___ me the next day.
why: In reported speech, 'will' becomes 'would', and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

context: Sara asked, "Where did you spend the weekend?"
prompt: Sara asked me where I ___ the weekend before.
why: In reported speech, 'did you spend' moves one step back to 'had spent'.

context: Yesterday at work, your boss asked, "Have you finished the report?"
prompt: My boss asked me ___ the report yet.
why: Reported yes/no questions use 'if' and normal word order, with no question order and no 'did'.

context: Last Friday, Ben said, "I can't come, I'm sick."
prompt: Ben said he ___ come to the party because he ___ sick.
why: Both verbs move back one step in reported speech: 'can't' becomes 'couldn't' and 'am' becomes 'was'.

context: Your sister said, "Don't touch my laptop!"
prompt: My sister told me ___ her laptop.
why: Reported orders use 'told someone to do' and for 'don't' use 'not to do'.

context: Your teacher announced the change to the whole class.
prompt: The teacher ___ us that the exam was moved to Monday.
why: 'Tell' needs a person right after it ('told us'). 'Said' would be 'said that' without 'us'.

context: Last year Lena said, "I've never been to Paris." She finally went there this summer.
prompt: Lena admitted she ___ to Paris before.
why: In reported speech, 'have been' moves back to 'had been'. It is no longer true now, so 'has' is wrong.

context: Yesterday, Omar said, "I'm busy today."
prompt: Yesterday Omar said he was busy ___.
why: When we report it later, 'today' changes to 'that day' because the time has moved.

context: Dana came home and found her kitchen floor covered in water.
prompt: When Dana got back from work, she realized that the pipe ___ all afternoon.
why: The leaking started before she got home and went on until then, so we use the past perfect continuous.

context: Tom is telling a friend why he missed an important call yesterday.
prompt: I ___ a shower when you called, so I didn't hear the phone.
why: The shower was in progress at the exact moment the phone rang, so we use the past continuous.

context: Noa arrived at the station last Friday and talked about her trip.
prompt: By the time Noa got to the station, the train ___ and she had to wait an hour for the next one.
why: The train left before she arrived. The earlier action in the past needs the past perfect.
